newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka army battles rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka army battles rights abuses.

text.p: Scores of Tamils remain missing in Sri Lanka's war-battered northern Jaffna peninsula but the human rights situation has improved, diplomats and aid workers said on Tuesday.

Colombo-based diplomats and aid workers who monitor the peninsula, captured by government troops earlier this year, support Tamil politician Joseph Pararajasingham's estimate that 300 people have disappeared in the past three months.

The military, fighting an ethnic war against the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, has been accused by the Tigers and human rights groups of arbitrary arrests, illegal detentions and other rights abuses, including murder and rape.

The army recaptured Jaffna city last December from the Tigers -- who had held the city for most of the past 13 years -- and has regained control of almost the entire peninsula, home to almost 500,000 people.
Lise Boudreault, Jaffna chief of the International Committee of the Red Cross, said there were still abuses, but the situation was improving.
"Generally speaking, the relations between the civilian population and the army are getting pretty good," she said.
"On the other side, you will see some misbehaviour. Soldiers are a bit under pressure here... They are nervous about grenades or things (that) can happen any time."
Boudreault said the military had followed up cases of abuses, including rape and murder.
"I would say in almost all those cases that the soldiers who were responsible for that have been prosecuted," she said.
A senior military official in Jaffna said human rights abuses were isolated and committed by rogue soldiers.
The army was committed to punishing misbehaviour and investigating all reported disappearances, said the official, who did not want to be named.
"We are not going to hide anything," he said.
Colombo's second most senior civil servant in the province, Thuraiappah Vythilinkam, said 174 people remained unaccounted for out of 749 reported disappearances since May.
A Western diplomat in Colombo said closer monitoring and an improving security situation in Jaffna were helping reduce abuses.
"They are cleaning up their act," he said.
The army was working to restore infrastructure and essential services in Jaffna where life was slowly returning to normal, the senior military official said.
"But it's hard for many of these people... They have known nothing but war for most of their life," he said.
President Chandrika Kumaratunga recently postponed local elections due next April because of continuing insecurity and rebel opposition to the polls.
The military official estimated it would be at least six months before elections could be held.
At least 50,000 people have been killed throughout this majority-Sinhalese country in the LTTE's 13-year battle for a Tamil homeland in the north and east.
